text: Friday, one minute to seven. A feast on the rooftop, everyone there, and one empty stool beside Seoa.
Her phone ticks over to seven.
The door bangs open, and Jaeha stumbles in, holding up seven shaking fingers. Seven o'clock!
Zero seconds to spare. Seoa tries very hard not to smile. Sit down before it gets cold.
Up come the crew: Uncle Pyo with soju, Dami with her little daughter, the Jang brothers with their prototype chicken. Wings of Glory!
The table goes quiet. Moon Ahin, with Saebyeok carrying a giant fruit basket. Who invited the white one, asks Lyra. Jaeha did. She was passing, says Moon Ahin.
She perches on a plastic stool like it's a throne, Lyra glaring beside her. More pets, asks the landlady. Not pets, says Nib.
Seoa climbs onto her stool and raises her cup. To everyone who came back!
Every cup goes up, along with a juice box, a lettuce leaf and a fruit basket.
Jaeha picks up his chopsticks, and the tips won't meet.
Close, he tells his fingers. Why won't they close?
Seoa's smile goes out.
And Jaeha slides off his stool. Operator body: critical.
Saturday, three in the morning, a hospital ward. Seoa sleeps holding his hand. Nib keeps watch on the windowsill.
A window only he can see. Carry capacity exceeded fourteen times. Body rating: F. Next excess: cardiac risk.
He reads it line by line, like a contract.
And he smiles. Capacity, rating. They're numbers, and numbers can go up.
Nib, dry as dust: he fell off a stool. In front of the white one.
By morning, the doctor has scans. Bones, nerves, blood, all fine. Medically, nothing is wrong with him.
Then why can't he hold a spoon, Seoa demands. Stress, the doctor guesses.
Yerin's healing closes wounds. This isn't a wound. She can't find it.
The fruit basket's card: get well, you owe me a rim. M.A.
Then Choi, reluctantly: he knows someone. Not a doctor. Much worse.
She taught him how to carry people out of gates. If she's still alive.
Saturday night, Choi's van heads south down the expressway.
Jaeha sleeps, hands shaking even now. Borro is folded in half in the back. Why is everything here the wrong size? Borro is comfortable.
Busan, Sunday at dawn. At the edge of the harbour market, an orange tent stall glows.
Inside, a short, broad old woman stirs a giant pan of tteokbokki, her left arm battered steel.
Auntie, it's Dongmin, says Choi. She doesn't turn round. Still alive. Good. Sit down and eat.
Then she turns, ladle raised, gold tooth glinting. Geum Okran. Retired S-rank. The Wall of Busan.
She sizes him up. So this is the one who can't hold his chopsticks. Even Borro steps back.
She taps him with the ladle like a doctor's hammer. Shoulders, spine, hands: carried too much.
Then she presses it over his heart. This carried everything.
One tap on the forehead. The only part of him that works.
And then the verdict. Your head is S-rank. Your body is garbage.
Nib nods. Lyra nods. Even Borro nods. Choi hides a laugh behind his coffee.
She leans in. He takes their pain into a body never built to hold it, fourteen times too much. Next time, his heart stops.
Jaeha goes sharp. How does she know he carries anything? He never said.
She looks out at the sea. The last man she saw carry like that was ten years ago, the night the gates opened.
Ten years ago. The night Jaeha's mom and dad died.
But the ladle cuts him off. Eat first, questions after. No! Training after. Then questions.
Her steel hand wraps his shaking fingers round a hot cup of tteokbokki.
Then she lets go. Hold it. Don't spill a drop. That's set one.
Is this training or torture, asks Lyra. Yes, says Auntie Geum.
She slaps down a timetable: run the breakwater at four, carry ice at five, tteokbokki at six.
And after that, with a terrible, delighted grin: one more set. Then just one more.
She likes him, Choi whispers. How can he tell? She hasn't hit him with the ladle.
The ladle flies back over her shoulder and bonks Choi on the head.
And Jaeha laughs for the first time in days, without dropping the cup.
A window opens over the pan. New quest: the Wall of Busan. Train the Operator's body. Reward unknown.
He presses it with a trembling finger.
For one moment, his fingers close tighter round the cup, and the shaking eases.
He looks at Auntie Geum's back. When does set two start?
She grins at her pan without turning. It already has, kid. He's still holding the cup.
The sun comes up over the harbour, Borro's mossy back sticking out of the tent.
Auntie Geum steps out, ladle on her shoulder, and looks out to sea. The sea's restless today.
Her steel fingers clench and unclench, all by themselves.
Out on the water, everything is calm. Nothing wrong at all.
But down below the surface, the light turns gold, then blue, then dark.
On the seabed lies a ring of gate light three hundred metres across, sealed under an ancient lid of stone and steel.
One old steel plate shears its bolts. A crack opens, and violet light bubbles up through it.
And under the lid, something enormous slides past in the dark.
In the tent, Jaeha looks up. A red window: a sealed gate is failing, close by. Nib turns toward the sea.
Auntie Geum looks out at the bright, calm sea beside him. Drink your tteokbokki, kid. He's going to need a body.

High over Busan, the harbour shines in the morning sun. But far out on the horizon, a violet stain spreads across the calm sea. His body is garbage, and a seal is failing. One more set. Then just one more.
